unit.title: Attend to break downs in hazardous areas

summary: This unit teaches you to deal with breakdowns where flammable gas, vapour or dust may be present: fuel depots and service stations, LPG plants, rum distilleries, sugar factories, feed and flour mills, and sewage pumping stations. You will learn how hazardous areas are classified into zones, how ignition sources are controlled, how plant is isolated, drained, purged and gas-tested, how to choose between cold and hot repair methods, and how to work under permits, respond to emergencies and hand plant back safely.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It builds on the general breakdown skills of isolation, fault-finding and repair, and adds what changes when the air itself may explode. In a **hazardous area**, a spark from a grinder, a phone, a dropped spanner or a weld can ignite gas, vapour or dust that you cannot see or smell, with deadly results.

A Level 3 welder-fitter called to such a site must understand the hazard, follow the site's permit system exactly, choose the safest repair method, and lead a crew that never takes a short cut, however hard the plant is pushing to restart.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees and welder-fitters who carry out breakdown repairs at fuel, gas, process, agricultural and wastewater sites, as members or leaders of a repair crew.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on site
rows: Recognise hazardous areas
Know which gases, vapours and dusts can explode, where they collect, and why these places need special rules.
Read zones and Ex markings
Use the area classification drawing, and check that equipment brought in or fitted suits the zone.
Control ignition sources
Keep sparks, flames, hot surfaces, static and unsuitable equipment out of the zone.
Work under permits
Accept and keep to the permit to work and hot work permit, and know who is responsible for what.
Isolate, drain, purge and gas-free
Make lines and equipment safe with positive isolation, and control the hazards of purge gases.
Test the atmosphere
Plan and record gas tests, understand the readings, and stop work when the limits are passed.
Choose and carry out the repair
Prefer cold methods, and where hot work is unavoidable, put every control in place.
Handle emergencies
Respond correctly to gas alarms, fires and confined-space incidents.
Hand back and report
Inspect, leak test, restore isolations in order, close the permit, and record everything that proves the work was safe.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on hazardous areas, zones, dust, permits, gas testing, ignition sources, isolation, repair methods, hot work controls, confined spaces, Ex equipment, emergencies and return to service.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms and figures (for example the zone number, nitrogen, double block and bleed, bump test, gas free, %LEL to % by volume, purge volumes) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: planning the full response to a fuel-line breakdown on paper, with permits, isolations, purge volume and gas-test points; and a simulated hot work repair in a marked area, with a permit, gas tests, a fire watch, a stop when the reading rises, and a report.

blocks.note: This unit is about judgement under pressure. In every question ask: what could ignite, what could fuel it, and has the permit system proved it safe? If not, the work does not start.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A fire or explosion needs three things together: **fuel** (a flammable gas, vapour, mist or dust), **oxygen** (from the air) and an **ignition source**. In a hazardous area the fuel may be in the air around you, so the only thing between normal work and an explosion is keeping ignition sources away and keeping the fuel out of the work.

ul: A gas or vapour burns only when it is mixed with air between two limits. The **lower explosive limit (LEL)** is the weakest mixture that will burn; the **upper explosive limit (UEL)** is the richest.
Below the LEL the mixture is too lean to burn; above the UEL it is too rich. A rich mixture is **not** safe: as it leaks out and mixes with air it passes through the flammable range.
The **flash point** of a liquid is the lowest temperature at which it gives off enough vapour to be lit by a spark. A liquid above its flash point is giving off flammable vapour.
The **auto-ignition temperature** is the temperature at which a gas or vapour ignites on its own, with no spark: from a hot surface, for example.

head: Substance
Where you meet it
Flammable range in air (about)
Heavier or lighter than air
Points to know
rows: Petrol (gasoline) vapour
Service stations, fuel terminals, tank farms
Heavier: collects low
Flash point about −40 °C: gives off vapour at any temperature
LPG (propane and butane)
Cooking-gas filling plants, cylinder stores, hotels
about 2–10%
Heavier: flows into drains, pits and trenches
A smell is added so leaks can be noticed
Ethanol vapour
Rum distilleries and spirit stores
about 3.3–19%
Heavier
High-strength spirit gives off flammable vapour at normal Jamaican temperatures
Methane (natural gas, biogas, sewer gas)
Sewage plants and pumping stations, landfills, farm digesters
Lighter: collects under roofs and covers
No smell of its own
Hydrogen sulphide (H₂S)
Sewage, wastewater, some industrial processes
about 4–46%
Slightly heavier
Very toxic as well as flammable; smells of rotten eggs at low levels but deadens the sense of smell at higher levels
Hydrogen
Battery charging rooms
Much lighter
Very easy to ignite

blocks.p: Diesel and kerosene have higher flash points (kerosene from about 38 °C, diesel usually above 50 °C), but steel left in the Jamaican sun, a hot engine or welding heat can raise them above it. Treat them with respect too.

blocks.note: Published limits differ a little between sources. Use the figures on the site's data sheets or the SDS for the product, and the figures your permit gives.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Many solids burn violently when they are fine dust in a cloud: **sugar, flour, animal feed, maize starch, wood dust, coal**, and some metal dusts such as aluminium. A dust explosion needs fuel, oxygen and ignition, plus the dust **dispersed in a cloud** and usually **confined** (inside a casing, room or duct).

ul: A small first blast, or even a knock, can shake settled dust off beams and ledges into a cloud. That cloud can then explode far more violently: the **secondary explosion**, which causes most of the damage in dust accidents.
So housekeeping matters: a layer of dust only about as thick as a paper clip, spread over a large area, can be enough to feed a secondary explosion.
Dust lying on a hot surface (a bearing, a motor, a lamp) can smoulder and ignite at a lower temperature than a dust cloud.

blocks.h: Too little or too much oxygen

ul: **Oxygen enrichment** (more than the normal 21% or so) makes everything burn far more fiercely: clothing soaked in oxygen can burst into flame from a spark. Never use oxygen to "freshen" the air in a pit or vessel, or to blow dust off clothes.

**Oxygen deficiency** is caused by inert gases such as nitrogen, or by gases from rotting material, pushing the oxygen out. Too little oxygen can make a person collapse within a few breaths, with no warning.

blocks.note: Places in Jamaica that often have hazardous areas: fuel terminals and service stations, LPG filling plants, rum distilleries, sugar factories (bagging, conveyors, silos), flour and feed mills, alumina refineries (fuel and process areas), paint stores, battery rooms, and sewage pumping stations and treatment plants.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Zones, area classification and Ex equipment

blocks.p: A site with hazardous areas has an **area classification drawing**: a plan showing each zone and its extent. Before you plan any work, find out from that drawing which zone you will be in. If the zone is not marked on site, check the drawing with the site's operations staff; never assume a place is safe because there is no sign.

head: Zone
What it means
Typical examples
rows: Zone 0 (gas)
An explosive gas mixture is present all the time, or for long periods
The vapour space inside a fuel tank
Zone 1 (gas)
An explosive gas mixture is likely now and then in normal operation
Round pump seals, vents and filling points; inside pits next to fuel lines
Zone 2 (gas)
An explosive gas mixture is not expected in normal operation, and if it forms it lasts only a short time
The wider area round a Zone 1
Zone 20 (dust)
An explosive dust cloud is present all the time or for long periods
Inside silos, hoppers, running elevator casings, dust collectors
Zone 21 (dust)
An explosive dust cloud is likely now and then in normal operation
Round bagging points and filling or emptying points
Zone 22 (dust)
A dust cloud is not expected in normal operation and would not last long
Areas near Zone 21, or near ducts that could leak

blocks.note: Zone 0 and Zone 20 are the most hazardous; Zone 2 and Zone 22 the least. Outside the zones, the area is "non-hazardous" (sometimes called safe), but a leak can still spread there.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Sites designed to American codes may use **classes and divisions** instead of zones. Class I is for flammable gases and vapours, Class II for combustible dusts, Class III for fibres. **Division 1** means the hazard can be present in normal operation (it covers what zones call 0 and 1); **Division 2** means it is present only if something goes wrong (much like Zone 2).
Electrical and some mechanical equipment used in a zone must be built so that it cannot ignite the atmosphere. It carries an **Ex marking**. An example: **Ex db IIB T4 Gb**.

head: Part of the marking
What it tells you
Examples
rows: Ex
Built for explosive atmospheres
Always comes first
Protection type
How it is made safe
d: flameproof (an explosion inside is contained); e: increased safety; i: intrinsically safe (too little energy to ignite); p: pressurised; t: dust-tight enclosure
Group
Which gases or dusts it is suited to
IIA (propane, petrol), IIB (ethylene), IIC (hydrogen, acetylene). IIC equipment also suits IIB and IIA; IIB also suits IIA. Dusts: IIIA, IIIB, IIIC
Temperature class
The hottest its surface can get
Equipment protection level (EPL)
Which zones it may be used in
Ga: Zones 0, 1, 2. Gb: Zones 1 and 2. Gc: Zone 2 only. Da, Db, Dc for Zones 20, 21, 22

ul: Equipment for a zone must have an EPL that suits the zone, a group that covers the gas or dust, and a temperature class **cooler** than the area needs (for example a T3 or T4 motor where T2 is required). Petrol vapour can be ignited by a surface at roughly 250–280 °C, so equipment near petrol must be T3 (200 °C) or cooler.

Work on Ex equipment is done only by people trained and authorised for it. If you notice a cracked cover, a missing bolt, a damaged cable gland or paint over a flameproof joint, report it at once and do not touch or "fix" it yourself.
Phones, cameras, radios, torches, smart watches and battery tools are **not** safe in a zone unless they are certified for it. Leave them outside, or use certified ones the site provides.

sections.title: Sources of ignition and their control

head: Source
Examples
How it is controlled
rows: Hot work
Welding, gas cutting, grinding, brazing, heat guns
Avoid it by using cold methods; if it is unavoidable, a hot work permit, gas-free equipment, continuous gas testing and a fire watch
Mechanical sparks
Hammering, dropped steel tools, grinding, steel dragged on concrete, aluminium smeared on rusty steel and then struck
Careful working, tool lanyards at height, spark-resistant tools where the site asks (as an extra, never instead of gas testing)
Static electricity
Liquid flowing or splashing into a container, synthetic clothing, moving belts, people walking
Bond and earth containers and equipment, use metal containers, fill slowly from the bottom, wear antistatic clothing and footwear
Hot surfaces
Steam pipes, engine exhausts, overheating bearings and motors, lamps
Keep surfaces below the auto-ignition temperature; use equipment of the right temperature class; fix overheating parts
Electrical equipment
Ordinary tools, extension leads, work lamps, switches, phones
Only equipment certified for the zone; no plugging or unplugging inside the zone
Engines and vehicles
Engine-driven welders, compressors and generators, trucks, customers' cars
Keep them outside the zone, where the permit says; fit spark arrestors and engine shut-off devices where the site requires them
Smoking and naked flames
Cigarettes, lighters, matches
Banned; lighters and matches stay outside the site

ul: A **diesel engine** can suck flammable vapour in through its air intake and burn it as extra fuel. The engine then speeds up out of control (it "runs away") and cannot be stopped with its normal switch, while its hot exhaust and sparks can ignite the cloud. That is why engine-driven equipment stays well outside the zone.

**Spark-resistant tools** (copper-beryllium or aluminium-bronze) make weaker sparks than steel tools, but they can still spark and they do not make gas testing or the permit unnecessary. Dressing copper-beryllium tools makes a toxic dust: leave that to the tool supplier.
In some fuel and sour-gas equipment, iron sulphide scale can heat up and glow on its own when it dries in air. Keep scale wet and follow the site's procedure when opening such equipment.
**Flame-resistant, antistatic overalls**, worn fully fastened. Nylon and polyester build up static and melt onto the skin in a flash fire.
Antistatic safety footwear, so that static drains away through your feet.
A personal gas monitor where the site requires one, worn near the breathing zone.
The usual PPE for the task: eye and ear protection, gloves, a hard hat and, for welding, full welding PPE.

blocks.p: Breakdown work in a hazardous area is always controlled by the site's **permit-to-work system**. The permit is the written proof that the plant has been made safe, that the air has been tested, and that the right people know what is happening.

head: Person
Responsibilities
rows: Permit issuer (usually operations, the area authority)

Makes the plant safe: isolation, draining, purging and blinding; arranges the gas test; states the hazards, controls, gas limits and time limit on the permit; signs only when it is safe; removes isolations and closes the permit at the end
Permit acceptor (the crew leader)

Checks on site that every isolation and control listed is really in place; signs to accept; briefs the crew; keeps the work within the stated scope, place and time; stops work and goes back to the issuer if anything changes; hands the permit back when the area is clean and the crew is clear
Authorised gas tester
Tests with a bump-tested, in-date detector at the points and times the permit sets, and records every reading
Fire watch
Watches for fire during and after hot work, and does nothing else
Control room
Knows what work is going on, so plant is not started, alarms are understood and nearby operations are adjusted
Crew members
Authorised and trained for the work; follow the permit; stop and report anything unsafe

ul: **Permit to work** (general or cold work permit): for work that makes no flame or spark.
**Hot work permit**: for welding, cutting, grinding, brazing or anything else that makes heat or sparks.
**Confined space entry permit**: for entering tanks, pits, wet wells, silos and similar spaces.
**Isolation certificate**: lists every valve, blind and electrical isolation, with lock numbers.
**Gas test record**: each reading, the time, the test point and the tester's name.

blocks.h: A hot work permit in a hazardous area states

ul: The exact location, the zone and the work to be done.
The hazards, and the isolations made (or the isolation certificate number).
The gas test results, how often tests must be repeated, and the limits at which work stops.
The precautions: drains covered, combustibles removed, barriers, extinguishers, fire watch, habitat, and where the welding set and cylinders must stand.
The time it is valid from and to, and the emergency arrangements.
Signatures for issue, acceptance, extension, hand-back and the end of the fire watch.
When a permit's time runs out, **stop**, make the work safe and get it renewed by the issuer. Nobody may alter the times on a permit themselves or have someone else "sign an extension".
A gas alarm, an emergency or a change in conditions **suspends** the permit. Work restarts only when the issuer has re-checked the area, a new gas test is in limits, and the permit is re-validated.
Before work starts, the crew leader gives a toolbox briefing: the hazards, the permit conditions, the alarm sounds, the escape routes, the muster point and the wind direction (check the windsock).
Tell the control room before starting and when finishing, so that nobody restarts the plant or opens a valve on your section, and so that alarms caused by your work are understood.

blocks.note: If a manager pushes you to start welding before the gas test is done or the permit is signed, refuse politely and firmly, and explain: vapour you cannot see or smell could ignite and kill people, and stop the plant for far longer. Use the waiting time to set up barriers, covers and extinguishers so the work can start as soon as it is safe. Record the pressure in your report.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Before a line or vessel that held fuel is opened or worked on, the fuel and its vapour must be kept out. Operations staff isolate the section; the crew checks every isolation is in place before accepting the permit.

head: Method
How it works
How secure
rows: Single closed valve
One valve closed, locked and tagged
The weakest: valves can let fuel past (a "passing" valve)
Double block and bleed
Two valves closed, with the small drain or vent between them open to a safe place, so any leak past the first valve is seen and vented
Much better; used where the site requires it
Spade or blind
A solid steel plate fitted between two flanges, rated for the line pressure
Positive isolation: a physical barrier
Spectacle blind
A figure-of-eight plate: one end solid, one open. Turned to the solid end to isolate
Positive isolation, quick to change
Spool removed
A short section of pipe taken out and the open ends blanked
Positive isolation

flow: Operations stop the flow and close and lock the valves (double block and bleed where required)
The electrician isolates and locks off the pumps and any motor-operated valves
The section is drained into bonded and earthed containers or a closed drain system
Pressure is released and vented to a safe place
The section is purged with nitrogen, steam or water, as the site's procedure says
Blinds or spades are fitted where a positive break is needed
The inside and the surroundings are gas tested to prove the section is gas free
Every isolation is listed on the permit or isolation certificate

blocks.p: Volume of a pipe = π × radius² × length. Multiply by the number of volume changes the procedure asks for. Example: an 80 mm bore pipe, 25 m long, purged with 5 volumes: π × 0.04² × 25 = 3.142 × 0.0016 × 25 = 0.126 m³ per volume; × 5 = **0.63 m³** of nitrogen. Use the radius (half the bore) in metres.

ul: **Nitrogen** is used because it does not burn and pushes vapour out. But it has no smell and pushes out oxygen too: a few breaths in a nitrogen-rich space can make a person collapse without warning. Vent the purge to a safe place, test for oxygen near vents and openings, and never put your head into a purged pipe or vessel.
Never purge with **oxygen**. Do not blow air into a line full of vapour unless the procedure says so: it makes an explosive mixture inside the pipe.
Sludge, scale and residues inside a pipe or tank can give off vapour again when they are heated by a weld. "Gas free" at the start does not mean gas free for ever: keep testing.

blocks.p: Fuel flowing into a container builds up static electricity. Use a metal container, **bond** it to the pipe or pump and **earth** it before draining starts, keep the end of the hose low to avoid splashing, and fill slowly. Never drain fuel into a plastic bucket.
Gas testing is how the permit system proves the air is safe. It is done by a trained, authorised gas tester, with an instrument that has been checked.

ul: A **multi-gas detector** (often four-gas) usually measures flammable gas as **% LEL**, oxygen as % by volume, and toxic gases such as hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) and carbon monoxide (CO) in parts per million (ppm).
Before each day's use, the detector is given a **bump test**: a short exposure to a known test gas to prove the sensors respond and the alarms work. It is zeroed in clean air.
It must also be **calibrated** at the intervals the maker sets, with a record or certificate. A detector out of calibration, or that failed its bump test, is not used.

Many flammable sensors are **catalytic** (pellistor) types. They need oxygen to work: in a nitrogen-purged pipe or vessel they can read low, even zero, when vapour is present. Use an infrared (IR) flammable sensor, or the method the site's procedure gives, for inerted atmospheres. Catalytic sensors can also be damaged by silicones, lead and H₂S.
When sampling through a tube with a pump (into a pit, drain or pipe), allow the time the maker gives for the sample to reach the sensor before you read it.
At the work position itself, and inside the equipment being worked on.
**Low points** (drains, pits, trenches, sumps, valve chambers) for gases heavier than air, such as petrol vapour, LPG and H₂S.
**High points** (under roofs, canopies and covers) for gases lighter than air, such as methane and hydrogen.
At flanges, valves, vents and any openings nearby, and downwind of the work.
At the air intake of a welding habitat.
Before the permit is issued.
Immediately before work starts.
At the intervals the permit sets, or continuously with a fixed or personal monitor, throughout the work.
After every break, and after any change: in the wind, in plant operations nearby, or in the work.
At once if anyone smells anything or a nearby alarm sounds.
**% LEL** is the share of the way to the lower explosive limit. 100% LEL means the mixture can burn.
To change % LEL to % by volume: **% by volume = % LEL × LEL ÷ 100**. Example: methane has an LEL of 5% by volume; a reading of 20% LEL is 20 × 5 ÷ 100 = 1% methane by volume (10 000 ppm).
Normal air holds about **21% oxygen** (20.9%). Most detectors alarm below about 19.5% (too little) and above about 23.5% (too much). Outside these, nobody enters, and hot work stops.
Detectors are often set to alarm at about 10% LEL and 20% LEL, but a hot work permit may set a much lower limit (for example 0% or below 5% LEL). **The permit's figure is the one that counts.**

blocks.note: If any reading is above the permit limit, the work does not start. If readings rise during the work, **stop hot work at once**, make the equipment safe, withdraw, tell the permit issuer and find the source. Work restarts only when the permit is re-issued after a new test. Never "weld faster to finish" or open an oxygen valve to dilute the gas.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Every reading goes on the **gas test record** kept with the permit: the test point, the time, the reading for each gas, the instrument and its bump-test date, and the tester's name and signature. The record shows the work was done under safe conditions, and it is needed for the report.

sections.title: Choosing and carrying out the repair

head: Point
Cold work
Hot work
rows: What it is
Work that makes no flame, spark or hot surface: bolting, clamping, hand sawing, cold-cutting machines, replacing parts
Welding, gas cutting, brazing, grinding, or anything that makes heat or sparks
When to choose it
First choice, wherever it gives a safe, lasting repair approved by the engineer
Only when there is no safe cold method, for example to restore a structural support to full strength
Controls still needed
Permit, isolation where parts are opened, gas testing, suitable tools and clothing
All of the cold work controls, plus everything in the hot work list below

ul: Can the faulty item be **taken out of the zone** and repaired in the workshop? A pump can often be lifted out; a new bracket can be made in the workshop and bolted in.
Can the repair be **bolted** rather than welded: an engineered clamp, a bolted bracket on an existing lug?
Can a pipe be cut with a **cold-cutting** machine (with cutting fluid) instead of a grinder or torch?
Hot tapping and welding on lines in service are specialist work, never part of a general breakdown repair.

blocks.h: Hot work controls in a hazardous area

ul: A permit to work and a hot work permit, issued to authorised people.
The equipment isolated, drained, purged and gas free; blinds fitted where needed.
Gas tests before and during the work (continuous monitoring is best), with clear stop rules.
Everything that can burn removed from the area that sparks can reach; what cannot be moved covered with fire blankets.
**Drains, gullies, trenches and openings covered** (fire blankets or mats), because vapour may sit in them and sparks fall into them.
Barriers and signs to keep people and vehicles out.
Screens to contain sparks and arc light.
Suitable extinguishers (for fuel fires, usually dry powder or foam) and fire blankets at the work.
A **fire watch** during the work and for the set time afterwards.
The welding set, engine-driven equipment and gas cylinders **outside the zone**, where the permit says; the work return clamp next to the weld.
A trained person whose **only** job during the hot work is to watch for fire. He or she does not weld, hold plates, fetch tools or fill in paperwork.
Before work: checks that combustibles are cleared, drains and gaps covered, extinguishers ready, and knows how to raise the alarm.

During work: watches where sparks and hot slag land, including below gratings, behind walls and inside openings; keeps people away; stops the work if there is fire, smoke, a gas alarm or anything unsafe; puts out small fires if it is safe to do so.

After work: stays for the time the permit sets (often 30 to 60 minutes, longer in high-risk areas), because smouldering material can flare up later; then checks the whole area again and signs the permit.

blocks.p: Where hot work must be done while the plant keeps running, a **welding habitat** may be used: a fire-resistant enclosure kept at a slightly higher pressure than outside by air drawn from a safe area. The pressure keeps sparks in and outside gas out. Gas detectors at the air intake and inside shut off the welding power automatically if gas is detected or the pressure is lost, and a trained attendant watches it.

ul: Stop and isolate the plant so that no fresh dust is made, and get the permits.

Remove dust layers from the equipment, beams, ledges and nearby surfaces with a **vacuum cleaner suited to combustible dust**, or gentle wet methods. **Never blow dust off with compressed air** or sweep hard: that makes the very cloud you must avoid.
Cover or seal openings into hoppers, ducts, elevators and silos so sparks cannot fall in.
Look for the ignition source that caused the breakdown: an overheated bearing, a slipping or misaligned elevator belt rubbing the casing, or a hot motor can ignite dust.
After hot work, the fire watch checks inside casings, hoppers and ducts as well as outside, for smouldering dust.
Smouldering dust is put out gently (a fine water spray, or as the site's procedure says). A strong jet or an extinguisher blast can throw the dust into the air and cause an explosion.

blocks.p: Tanks, pits, wet wells, sewers, silos and large ducts are **confined spaces**: enclosed places where gas, lack of oxygen, or engulfment can kill. Many deaths are of people who went in to rescue someone else.

ul: Enter only if there is no other way to do the job, under a **confined space entry permit**, after isolation, cleaning and ventilation.
Test the atmosphere from **outside** before entry, at the top, middle and bottom, for oxygen, flammable gas and toxic gases, and keep monitoring while people are inside.

A trained **attendant** (standby person) stays at the entrance the whole time, keeps in contact with the people inside and keeps count of them, and raises the alarm and starts the rescue plan if anything goes wrong, **without going in**.
A rescue plan and equipment (harness and lifeline, tripod and winch, breathing apparatus) must be ready before entry.
Only trained people enter, using equipment certified for the zone.

sections.title: Emergencies, return to service and reporting

flow: Stop work at once
Make safe only if it takes seconds: stop welding, close cylinder valves
Leave by the agreed escape route, upwind or across the wind, away from the release (check the windsock)
Go to the muster point and take a head count
Tell the control room or the permit issuer
Do not return until the all-clear is given and a new gas test is in limits; the permit must be re-validated

ul: Never stay to finish a weld, and never go looking for the leak yourself.
If someone collapses in a pit or tank, raise the alarm and start the rescue plan. Do not go in without breathing apparatus and the rescue team.
For a fire, raise the alarm; fight it only if it is small, you are trained and you have a safe escape behind you.

flow: Inspect the repair: the weld or bolted joint, gaskets, bolts and supports
Check any Ex equipment that was disturbed: covers, bolts, glands and seals all correct
Clear tools, rags, waste and spare parts from the area
The fire watch completes the set time after hot work, and the area is checked again
Operations remove blinds and spades and restore the isolations in the right order, under the permit
Leak test the line or joint, as the procedure says, before full flow is let in
Gas test around the work; tell the control room
The permit is signed off and closed, and the area handed back

head: Record
Why it matters
rows: The fault and its cause
So repeat failures (such as a pump seal that keeps failing) can be traced to the real cause: misalignment, worn bearings, vibration, running dry
The repair method and parts, including Ex details of anything replaced
So the site's equipment register stays correct and replacement parts stay certified
The permits, isolations and gas test readings, with times
Proof that the work was done under safe conditions
The tests after the repair (leak test, test run)
Proof that the plant was safe to restart
The downtime and its cost
For the site's cost and reliability records
Recommendations
For example a better seal type, more frequent checks, better dust housekeeping, or guarding a hose

ul: Cost of a stoppage = hours stopped × the cost per hour. A pump down for 3 h 30 min at J$80 000 an hour costs 3.5 × 80 000 = J$280 000.
Purge volumes and % LEL conversions, as shown in the earlier sections.
Permit times: a permit valid for 6 hours from 07:30 runs out at 13:30, and work stops then unless it is renewed.

blocks.note: Production losses are real, but they can be recovered. Lives and plant destroyed by an explosion cannot. Every step in this unit exists because someone, somewhere, was killed without it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can explain why fuel depots, distilleries, mills, LPG plants and sewage stations need special rules for breakdown work.
I can explain LEL, UEL, flash point and auto-ignition temperature.
I can say where heavy and light gases collect, and name the extra danger of hydrogen sulphide.
I can explain how dust explosions and secondary explosions happen.
I can describe gas Zones 0, 1 and 2 and dust Zones 20, 21 and 22, and read an area classification drawing.
I can read an Ex marking and say whether equipment suits a zone, gas group and temperature class.
I can name the sources of ignition and how each one is controlled, including static and diesel engines.
I can say what the permit issuer, the crew leader, the gas tester and the fire watch are each responsible for.
I can explain what to do when a permit runs out or is suspended.
I can describe isolation by double block and bleed, spades and spectacle blinds, and say why a single valve is weakest.
I can work out a purge volume and explain the hazards of nitrogen.
I can drain fuel safely, with bonded and earthed containers.
I can say how a detector is bump tested and calibrated, and why a catalytic sensor can under-read in nitrogen.
I can plan gas test points and times, convert % LEL to % by volume, and apply the permit's stop rules.
I can choose a cold repair method before hot work, and list the controls hot work needs.
I can describe the fire watch's duties and why it stays after the work ends.
I can control dust before, during and after a repair in a mill or factory.
I can describe the controls for entering a confined space and the attendant's role.
I can respond correctly to a gas alarm.
I can hand plant back after a repair and write a report that records the proof of safe work.

terms: Area classification drawing
A site plan showing the hazardous zones and their extent
Auto-ignition temperature
The temperature at which a gas or vapour ignites with no spark
Bonding and earthing
Connecting containers and equipment together and to earth so static cannot build up
Bump test
A short exposure of a detector to test gas, to prove its sensors and alarms work
Cold work
Work that makes no flame, spark or hot surface
Confined space
An enclosed space where gas, lack of oxygen or engulfment can kill
Double block and bleed
Two closed valves with the drain between them open, to show and vent any leak
Ex marking
The marking that shows equipment is built and certified for explosive atmospheres
Fire watch
A trained person whose only task is to watch for fire during and after hot work
Flash point
The lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off vapour that can be lit
Gas free
Proved by testing to hold no flammable gas or vapour
Gas test record
The record of every gas reading, its time, place and tester
Hazardous area
A place where an explosive atmosphere of gas, vapour or dust may be present
Hot work
Welding, cutting, grinding, brazing or other work that makes heat or sparks
LEL
Lower explosive limit: the weakest mixture of a gas in air that will burn
Nitrogen purge
Pushing vapour out of a pipe or vessel with nitrogen, which does not burn
Positive isolation
A physical break, such as a spade, blind or removed spool
Secondary explosion
A larger dust explosion fed by dust shaken into the air by a first blast
Spade (blind)
A solid steel plate fitted between flanges to shut off a pipe
Spectacle blind
A figure-of-eight plate, one end solid and one open, turned to isolate a line
Temperature class
The highest surface temperature of Ex equipment, from T1 (450 °C) to T6 (85 °C)
UEL
Upper explosive limit: the richest mixture of a gas in air that will burn
Welding habitat
A pressurised, fire-resistant enclosure for hot work in a running plant
Zone
A class of hazardous area: 0, 1, 2 for gas; 20, 21, 22 for dust

c1.title: A cracked pump bracket at a rum distillery in Clarendon
c1.text: At a rum distillery in Clarendon, the pump that transfers high-strength spirit (about 90% alcohol) has worked loose because its steel mounting bracket has cracked. The area drawing shows the pump in a Zone 1 area, rated for gas group IIB and temperature class T2. The pump's motor is also to be replaced, and stores offer one marked Ex db IIB T3 Gb. Rohan, the crew leader, has brought a mains work lamp and a battery impact wrench from the workshop.

c2.title: A broken pump rail in a wet well in Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: At a sewage pumping station in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, one submersible pump has stopped in a wet well about 6 m deep, and a bracket on its guide rail near the bottom is broken. The pumps can be lifted out on their guide rails with the station's hoist. Nadine leads the crew. When the cover is opened, a crew member smells rotten eggs, but a few minutes later says the smell has gone. Before anyone goes in, the tester's meter reads 19.0% oxygen near the bottom of the well.

c3.title: A seized elevator bearing at a feed mill in St Catherine
c3.text: At an animal-feed mill in St Catherine, the head bearing of a bucket elevator overheated and seized, and the elevator stopped. A cracked bracket on the elevator boot must also be welded. Fine feed dust lies about 3 mm deep on the elevator casing and on the beams and ledges around it.

c4.title: Opening a petrol line at a Kingston fuel terminal
c4.text: At a fuel terminal on the Kingston waterfront, a cracked support on a petrol line must be repaired, and a section of the line has to be opened. Operations will isolate and drain the 150 mm bore section, 40 m long, and purge it with three times its volume of nitrogen. The crew takes the LEL of petrol vapour as 1.4% by volume. After purging, the crew's catalytic-bead detector reads 0% LEL inside the pipe. A diesel-driven air compressor has been parked beside the pipe track.

c5.title: Welding a canopy column at a service station in St Ann's Bay
c5.text: At a service station in St Ann's Bay, St Ann, the corroded base plate of a canopy column must be repaired by welding, about 6 m from the nearest pump island. The station manager wants to keep all the pumps selling during the repair, and customers' cars keep driving onto the forecourt. The hot work permit says the fire watch stays for 60 minutes after hot work ends; the welding finishes at 15:10.

questions.q: Why is the distillery's pump area treated as hazardous, when the spirit is made to be drunk?
o: The pumps are heavy and can crush a fitter's hands during removal
Strong spirit gives off vapour that ignites at room temperature
Spilt spirit makes the floor round the pump wet and slippery
Alcohol vapour poisons anyone who breathes it for a few minutes
questions.why: Spirit at about 90% alcohol has a flash point well below normal Jamaican temperatures, so it is always giving off vapour that can ignite. The other hazards are real, but they are not what makes it a hazardous area.

questions.q: Where should the cracked bracket be repaired?
o: In place, with the pump left running so no output is lost
In place, with the welder keeping a very low current
In the pump room doorway, where there is more light and air
In the workshop outside the zone, once the pump is off
questions.why: Taking the item out of the zone turns hot work in a hazardous area into ordinary workshop work. The new or repaired bracket is then brought back and bolted in, which is cold work.

questions.q: Is the motor marked Ex db IIB T3 Gb suitable for this pump?
o: No: a T3 motor may run hotter than a T2 area allows
No: only Ga equipment, made for Zone 0, may be used in Zone 1
Yes: Gb suits Zone 1, IIB matches, and T3 is cooler than T2
No: a flameproof db motor is made only for combustible dust
questions.why: Gb equipment may be used in Zones 1 and 2; group IIB covers the area's IIB gases; and T3 limits the surface to 200 °C, below the 300 °C of T2. A higher T number means a cooler surface.

questions.q: What should Rohan do with the mains work lamp and the battery impact wrench?
o: Take them out unless they are certified for the zone
Use them, keeping them at least a metre from the pump
Use them, as the pump has been switched off and locked
Use only the battery wrench, as it has no cable to spark
questions.why: Ordinary lamps and battery tools can spark inside, and switching off the pump does not remove vapour from the area. Only equipment certified for the zone, or allowed by the permit after gas testing, is used.

questions.q: How should the crew deal with the stopped pump itself?
o: Lift it out on its rails and work on it at the surface
Send a fitter down to repair it where it stands in the well
Lower a welding lead and repair it at the bottom of the well
Pump the well dry and repair it at the bottom
questions.why: The guide rails exist so pumps can be lifted out. Working at the surface keeps people out of the confined space and the hazardous atmosphere; entry is only for work that cannot be done any other way, such as the rail bracket.

questions.q: What should Nadine make of the rotten-egg smell fading?
o: The gas has blown away, so the well is now safe to enter
High H₂S levels deaden the sense of smell; trust the meter
The smell came from the sewage, not from any gas at all
Rotten-egg smells are harmless; only methane really matters
questions.why: Hydrogen sulphide is toxic and flammable. At higher levels it stops you smelling it, so a fading smell can mean more gas, not less. Only the detector tells you the level.

questions.q: During the entry to fix the rail bracket, what is the attendant's job?
o: Climb down to help as soon as the entrant seems to struggle
Leave once the entrant has reached the bottom of the well safely
Stay outside, keep contact and call for help without entering
Carry out the gas tests and set up the welding equipment as well
questions.why: The attendant watches, keeps contact and count, and starts the rescue plan if something goes wrong. Untrained rescuers who go in are a common cause of second and third deaths in confined spaces.

questions.q: What should happen after the 19.0% oxygen reading?
o: Enter, since 19% is close to the 21% in normal air
Enter quickly, before the level can drop any lower
Enter wearing a dust mask over the nose and mouth
No entry: ventilate, find the cause and test again
questions.why: Below about 19.5% oxygen nobody enters. Something is using up or pushing out the oxygen, and a dust mask gives no protection. Ventilate, find the cause and retest before any entry.

questions.q: How should the crew remove the feed dust before work starts?
o: With a leaf blower set to its very lowest speed
With a vacuum cleaner made for combustible dust
With a stiff yard broom, working as quickly as possible
With a hose jet, washing it all into the drains
questions.why: Blowing or brisk sweeping lifts the dust into a cloud, the very thing that explodes. A vacuum suited to combustible dust, or gentle wet methods, removes it without making a cloud.

questions.q: Why is the overheated head bearing itself an ignition hazard in the mill?
o: A hot surface can ignite a dust layer or a dust cloud
It only damages the shaft, so it cannot start any fire
Its heat dries out the feed so that it spoils more quickly
It sets off the mill's smoke alarms for no good reason
questions.why: Dust settled on a hot bearing can smoulder and ignite at a lower temperature than a dust cloud, and a burning layer can ignite a cloud inside the casing. Overheating bearings and rubbing belts are classic causes of elevator explosions.

questions.q: Which zone is the inside of the elevator casing likely to be while it runs?
o: Zone 21
Zone 20
Zone 22
Zone 1
questions.why: Inside a running elevator, dust is in the air all the time, which is Zone 20. Zone 21 is for clouds now and then, such as round a bagging point; Zone 1 is a gas zone.

questions.q: After welding the boot bracket, why does the fire watch also check inside the elevator casing?
o: To make sure that no tools have been left inside the casing
To check that all the bucket bolts are tight before restart
Sparks or slag may have fallen in and set dust smouldering
Because the permit has to list every part of the mill checked
questions.why: Hot particles fall through openings and lie hidden in dust, where they can smoulder unseen and flare up later. The fire watch checks wherever sparks could have gone, inside as well as outside.

questions.q: How much nitrogen is needed for the purge?
o: About 2.12 m³
About 0.71 m³
About 8.48 m³
About 21.2 m³
questions.why: One volume = π × r² × L = 3.142 × 0.075² × 40 = 0.707 m³; three volumes = 2.12 m³. Using the 0.15 m bore as the radius gives four times too much.

questions.q: A reading of 25% LEL is taken at a flange near the work. What share of the air there is petrol vapour?
questions.why: % by volume = % LEL × LEL ÷ 100 = 25 × 1.4 ÷ 100 = 0.35%. That is a quarter of the way to a burnable mixture: far above any hot work limit, so welding stops.

questions.q: Why should the crew not trust the 0% LEL reading inside the purged pipe?
o: Nitrogen makes detectors over-read, so the true figure is lower
Catalytic sensors measure only oxygen, not any flammable gas
Readings inside pipes are never reliable, whatever the sensor
A catalytic sensor needs oxygen, so it can read low in nitrogen
questions.why: Catalytic sensors burn a trace of the gas on a heated bead, which needs oxygen. In an inerted pipe they can show zero when vapour is present. An infrared sensor, or the site's procedure for inerted spaces, is needed.

questions.q: What should be done about the diesel compressor by the pipe track?
o: Leave it, as diesel is much harder to ignite than petrol is
Leave it running, but keep its engine at low revs throughout
Leave it there, as it will not be used for any of the hot work
Move it out of the zone, as it could draw in vapour and race
questions.why: A diesel engine can suck in petrol vapour as fuel and run away out of control, and its hot exhaust and sparks are ignition sources. Engines stay outside the zone, where the permit says.

questions.q: The station manager wants all pumps selling during the repair. What should be agreed?
o: The nearby pumps and any tanker delivery stop during hot work
All pumps keep selling, and drivers are asked not to smoke
Selling goes on, and welding stops whenever a car is at a pump
Selling goes on, as 6 m is a safe distance from any pump
questions.why: Fuelling and deliveries release petrol vapour, which is heavier than air and drifts across the forecourt. Hot work goes ahead only with nearby dispensing and deliveries stopped, as the permit sets out.

questions.q: What should be done about customers' cars on the forecourt?
o: Let them in, as long as the drivers switch off their engines
Ask a pump attendant to wave the cars past the welder
Close that part of the forecourt with barriers and signs
Weld only between cars, stopping each time one arrives
questions.why: Vehicles are ignition sources and bring people into the spark zone. Barriers and signs keep them out of the work area for the whole job; relying on drivers or on stopping and starting is not control.

questions.q: When may the fire watch end and the permit be signed off?
o: At 15:10, as soon as the welding stops
At 15:40, as 30 minutes is enough outdoors
At 16:10, after a final check of the area
As soon as the base plate has cooled down
questions.why: The permit sets 60 minutes after hot work ends, so the watch runs to 16:10. Smouldering material can flare up long after the plate looks cold; the area is checked again before signing.

questions.q: An American-designed fuel terminal marks an area "Class I, Division 1". What should a crew used to zones understand from this?
o: Combustible dust may form a cloud there now and then in normal work
Flammable gas or vapour can be present in normal operation
Gas or vapour would be present there only after a rare failure
Only one kind of flammable fuel is stored or handled in that area
questions.why: Class I covers flammable gases and vapours; Division 1 means the hazard can exist in normal operation, covering what the zone system calls Zones 0 and 1. Division 2 is the abnormal-only case, like Zone 2.
